edges.relationship: Kindi identifies Kuhn’s use of Wittgenstein’s family resemblances to explain the cohesion of normal research, while disputing his interpretation.
edges.evidence_note: Named substantive scholar Vasso Kindi, 2017:595–597, discusses Structure 1970:44–45 and the Cavell reading route. She finds Kuhn’s natural-families reading mistaken while recognizing a productive model for shared practice. The origin of the word paradigm is expressly disputed; no claim that Wittgenstein generated Kuhn’s whole theory or that the two met. Kuhn’s chapter V, Wittgenstein’s original and the underlying Cavell memoir/interview remain unread in this continuation.

edges.relationship: Pirozelli reports Kuhn’s objection that Foucault’s account does not adequately explain transitions between epistemes.
edges.evidence_note: Named substantive scholar Paulo Pirozelli, 2021:298–300, reads the Borradori interview cited as 1991:160–161. He distinguishes Kuhn’s limited knowledge of Foucault, shared concern with historically changing language and non-teleological science, and disagreement over the explanation of change. This is an explicitly mediated, bounded objection, not a claim that Kuhn refuted all of Foucault. The original interview and books remain unread; no influence is inferred from resemblance between paradigm and episteme.

edges.relationship: Nora credits Ariès’s Historien du dimanche with inspiring his idea of ego-history.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2022 answer about editorial regrets explicitly identifies Ariès’s Historien du dimanche as the inspiration, separately mentioning his admiration for Le temps de l’histoire. He regrets not publishing Ariès and says he came to know him too late; admiration, publishing and personal acquaintance are not collapsed. This is a retrospective intellectual acknowledgment, not new reading of either original or proof that Ariès supplied every aspect of the later collective project. The current page’s later memorial heading is distinct from the dated 1 December 2022 conversation.

edges.relationship: Nora recalls encouraging Furet to gather dispersed articles into Penser la Révolution française.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2022 answer to the question on moving a generation from articles to books explicitly confirms the editorial intervention and names Furet’s volume, alongside separate Le Goff, Bottéro and Gernet examples. This is a specific act of scholarly editorial assembly, not proof that Nora authored the articles, endorsed every argument or originated Furet’s interpretation. The complete volume and private editorial correspondence are unread; the earlier Furet graph records remain unchanged.

edges.relationship: Nora credits Le Goff’s invitations to additional historians with expanding their planned small project into Faire de l’histoire’s collective volumes.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2022 collective-work answer describes an initial small group including Foucault, Le Roy Ladurie, Furet, Le Goff and Nora, then identifies Le Goff’s repeated invitations as a reason the undertaking expanded. This is a bounded collaborative contribution to a shared historiographic project, not sole Le Goff authorship or a single doctrine imposed on every contributor. Existing opposite Nora-to-Le Goff edge_1661 concerns the later Saint Louis source encounter and remains distinct.

edges.relationship: Darnton credits Thompson’s history-from-below perspective with stimulating his attempt to reconstruct ideas from the literary underground.
edges.evidence_note: Own published Spanish 2024 formation answer explicitly calls Thompson’s perspective stimulating and links it to his decision to study Grub Street writers. This is an acknowledged methodological debt, distinct from Cobb’s inspiration, Shackleton’s tutoring and Harry Pitt’s advice about theoretical scaffolding. No particular Thompson title or exact date of reading is supplied; the early-1960s context does not authorize inventing a 1963-book reading before publication. Originals and private supervision records remain unread.

edges.relationship: Darnton explicitly names Bourdieu among thinkers whose ideas provide scaffolding for his historical writing.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2024 theory answer twice identifies Bourdieu and says he borrows ideas while often leaving theoretical frameworks implicit. The acknowledgment is shared with Geertz, Goffman, Douglas and Turner, not exclusive formation or adoption of every Bourdieusian thesis. He specifies no original Bourdieu title here; none is supplied or newly read. His own historical narratives are distinguished from the interviewer’s suggestions.

edges.relationship: Darnton acknowledges borrowing Douglas’s ideas when developing his anthropological approach to historical meaning.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2024 theory answer expressly identifies Mary Douglas among borrowed intellectual resources. Own 2021 anthropology answer gives her pangolin as a concrete example of meaningful things woven into ritual and cultural patterns, alongside Turner and Evans-Pritchard. This is a plural, critically interpreted debt, not formal instruction or identification of an unread original Douglas title. Darnton rejects a mechanical anthropological toolkit.

edges.relationship: Darnton uses Goffman’s definition of situations to interpret theatrical metaphors and collective perceptions in prerevolutionary Paris.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2021 answer names The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life and distinguishes an initial superficial role-playing reading from a later, more useful account of defining a situation. He connects it specifically to accounts of 1787–1788 and a work then in progress. Own 2024 answer confirms theatrical communication as a resource for The Revolutionary Temper. This is his attributed use, not independent verification of Goffman’s book or every historical episode.

edges.relationship: Darnton credits Durkheim’s collective-consciousness concept when explaining The Revolutionary Temper’s account of shared historical perceptions.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2024 theory answer explicitly attributes collective consciousness to Durkheim and says he made this theoretical acknowledgment more visible because the book’s title required explanation. This is a specific conceptual resource rather than a claim that all readers think alike, a verified single cause of revolution, or adherence to an entire sociological school. No particular original Durkheim work is identified or newly read; the existing group Social facts and collective life node is distinct from the person endpoint.

edges.relationship: Darnton credits Furet’s group with drawing him into serial book history while extending its source base to illegal literature.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2021 opening answer says he absorbed long-term structural and statistical history, names Furet’s histoire sérielle and dates his introduction to the Livre et société group to 1972. His own illegal-book research had begun earlier and supplied material absent from that project. The 2024 book-history answer separately recalls the encounter and later friendships. This is a bounded methodological and collaborative debt, not sole origination of his research, identical archives or fresh reading of the collective volumes. The Spanish witness’s century-title wording is not silently used as a corrected bibliography.

edges.relationship: Darnton credits Chartier’s work on readers’ active appropriation while retaining doubts about the evidentiary reach of reading history.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2021 reading-history answer explicitly says he follows Chartier in taking inspiration from de Certeau and the other named reader theorist. He is persuaded by Chartier’s insights while distinguishing suggestive findings from a fully documented history. This resource coexists with his particular criticism and the 2024 insistence on substantial shared ground. The source’s spelling of the second intermediary is not treated as a new identity; no Chartier book or original discussion is freshly read.

edges.relationship: Darnton questions the evidence available for a systematic history of reading and disputes the claim that the Revolution invented the Enlightenment.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2021 answer praises Chartier’s insights but says sparse sources leave aperçus rather than a demonstrated history of reading. Own 2024 answer recounts their disagreement over The Cultural Origins of the French Revolution, maintaining that an Enlightenment force existed before 1789 while agreeing that later revolutionary legitimation mattered. He explicitly rejects simple book-to-action causation for both scholars and is unsure they have a fundamental difference. These are particular, dated objections in a friendly exchange, not rejection of all Chartier research or a fresh reading of his book.

edges.relationship: Darnton explicitly takes inspiration from de Certeau’s active reader, through his engagement with Chartier’s work.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2021 reading-history answer identifies Chartier’s mediation and de Certeau’s account of readers finding meanings unintended by authors. This is a named acknowledged resource, shared with another reading theorist, not a claim that readers escape every material constraint. Darnton’s following doubts about generalization and evidence remain explicit. No exact original de Certeau title or newly read book is supplied.

edges.relationship: Darnton asks how the reader-as-poacher model can yield demonstrable collective tendencies rather than endlessly varied individual readings.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2021 reading-history answer raises the problem conditionally after explicitly crediting de Certeau. He considers Fish’s interpretive communities as a possible response, then asks how they can be located with evidence. This is a particular limit on the historical application of the model, not a claim that de Certeau denied social pattern or that Chartier endorses absolute reader freedom. The existing group route preserves Chartier’s own rejection of that absolute-freedom interpretation; original books remain unread.

edges.relationship: Darnton uses Anderson’s account of shared reading and collective consciousness to reconsider the eighteenth-century French reading public.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2021 answer explicitly pairs Anderson with Gustave Tarde as recently helpful resources, describes Anderson’s colonial-nationalism argument, then develops his own Ancien Régime application. This is a bounded comparative resource, not an assertion that the two settings are equivalent or a guessed reading of a particular Anderson title. Individual variation and collective participation coexist; original works and Darnton’s entire later book remain unread.

edges.relationship: Darnton invokes Lévi-Strauss’s account of thinking with concrete things when explaining his interpretive approach to historical cultures.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2021 anthropology answer explicitly credits the demonstration that people combine concrete things in thought, then gives distinct Douglas, Turner and Evans-Pritchard examples. This is his specific conceptual resource, not adherence to all structuralism or evidence that each anthropologist offered an interchangeable method. He insists on evidence and the possibility of interpretive error and rejects mechanical instruments for unlocking symbols. No exact original Lévi-Strauss book is named or newly read.

edges.relationship: Darnton challenges the applicability of Habermas’s rational public sphere to eighteenth-century Parisian songs, rumors and noisy exchanges.
edges.evidence_note: In his own published 2024 answer Darnton expresses admiration for Habermas while contrasting a sober rational-discussion model with shouting, singing, stories, market disputes, scandals and gossip in eighteenth-century France. The objection concerns historical application and forms of public communication, not a denial that public opinion existed. He identifies a sympathetic parallel criticism by Farge. Habermas’s original text and Farge’s original response are not newly read, and no exact original title is inferred.

edges.relationship: Darnton explicitly aligns his account of noisy Parisian public opinion with Farge’s sympathetic criticism of Habermas.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2024 answer says his perspective coincides with Farge’s criticism that Habermas misrepresents the public presentation of ideas: cafés and markets, songs, gossip, scandals and rumors rather than only sober rational discussion. This is a specific attributed methodological comparison, not proof that Farge caused Darnton’s approach or an independent reading of her original argument. Darnton preserves admiration for Habermas and the existence of public opinion.
